newsitem.title: USA: ADM, Cargill to accept Roundup Ready soy.
newsitem.headline: ADM, Cargill to accept Roundup Ready soy.

text.p: Cargill Inc and Archer Daniels Midland Co said Thursday they plan to accept soybeans grown from genetically altered seeds despite recent protests in Europe by several consumer groups.
"The plan is to accept the beans our farmers deliver us," said Linda Thrane, assistant vice-president of public affairs for Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc.
"The scientific testing is complete. The approvals (from Europe and Japan) are in. It's business as usual for now."
The seeds, known as Roundup Ready, allow farmers to safely spray Monsanto Co's popular Roundup brand herbicide.
"ADM will accept Roundup-ready soybeans," an ADM spokesperson said.
ADM/Growmark, a subsidiary of ADM, had said last spring it would not accept soybeans grown from transgenic seed until the seeds received international approval.
The European Union in March approved for import soybeans grown from the seeds.
But a European consumer group on Thursday warned that their members would avoid U.S. soybeans unless farmers separated the altered strains and gene-altered soy products were labeled.

About one to two percent of the 1996 U.S. soybean crop is transgenic and that includes product that is being grown for seed stock next year, said Jim Hershey, division director for Europe and the Middle East with the American Soybean Association in St. Louis.

"We are looking at approximately one to 1.5 million tonnes (37 to 50 million bushels) of Roundup Ready beans harvested this year out of current USDA and private estimates of 62 million tonnes (2.3 billion bushels)," he said.
A Central Soya Co spokesman was not available for comment.
USDA Under Secretary Gene Moos on Thursday repeated the U.S. stance that labelling for transgenic products would be both unnecessary and unworkable.
"There's no need for labelling. We see no reason why labelling should be required and we think it impossible on top of that," Moos told Reuters.
